newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany determined to cut deficit-Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Germany determined to cut deficit-Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday he had stressed to European Finance Ministers Germany's will to reduce its deficit to meet the target for the European single currency this year and that they had welcomed the plan.
Waigel said Britain would need to be in the European exchange rate mechanism for two years to join EMU but that he would not like to comment further on its intentions under the new Labour government.
He said Bonn would consider further budgetary measures if needed to meet the EMU targets based on the semi-annual tax estimate to be compiled later this week.

Waigel said public finances in Europe must be further consolidated so that the European Union members which do not yet meet the EMU deficit rule bring their deficits into line by the end of this year. He said the chances were good that this would occur.
Only five of the 15 EU members had 1996 deficits and debt levels in line with the requirements set by the Maastricht Treaty.
"Germany communicated its intention to meet the deficit criterion. This was expressly greeted within the framework of the (finance ministers') overall recommendation," Waigel said.

Asked if there were still a chance for Britain to join EMU at the start in 1999, Waigel said, "The problem is that the Maastricht Treaty requires two-year membership in a currency system, the ERM. We hold that as necessary under the treaty."

He also said that despite noteworthy economic growth and robust successes on the labour market, Britain's deficit was still above the EMU goal of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, and it has an "opt-out" on EMU.
Waigel said he had discussed Britain's plans briefly with the new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, whom he planned to meet soon with the aim of developing an "intensive cooperation".
Asked what he expected this week's tax estimate in Bonn to bring, he said, "In any case, we will decide appropriate measures based on the results of the tax estimate."

While private sector and opposition critics project tax revenues to be up to 20 billion marks below budget forecasts, Waigel declined to preempt the tax estimate, which will be announced on Thursday following consulatations by the federal and state governments, central bank and private-sector advisors.
He said that any comment he might make now could upset the delicate process of drawing up the estimate.
